summaries.example: Imagine the word “dog.” It can point to many different dogs, even though each dog is a separate animal. Sharpe asks whether something shared by all dogs exists in the world, exists only in our minds, or is connected to both.
summaries.summary: Johannes Sharpe was a philosopher and theologian who lived in the late Middle Ages. He worked mainly at Oxford and became an important member of the Oxford Realists, a group influenced by John Wyclif. A major question for Sharpe was the problem of universals: when many things are alike, is there a real shared nature among them? Sharpe answered that universals can be real in things and can also appear in thought and language. He was still willing to learn from nominalist objections, especially the idea that words and thoughts do not copy the world exactly. Sharpe also wrote about identity, difference, the soul, knowledge, and Aristotle’s study of nature. His work shows how philosophers can defend one broad view while changing parts of it after hearing strong criticisms.
key_ideas: Sharpe was a late-medieval philosopher connected with the Oxford Realists.
He defended universals as real, while also accepting some criticisms made by nominalist thinkers.
He said that language and the world are connected, but they do not match in a simple one-to-one way.
He studied universals, meaning, identity, knowledge, the soul, and nature.
summaries.why_it_matters: Sharpe’s questions help us notice that ordinary words can be surprisingly complicated. A word such as “human” applies to many people, but each person is also an individual. Thinking about this can help us understand how language, ideas, and the world fit together. Sharpe also shows that a thinker can disagree with a school of philosophy while still learning from its arguments.

important_terms.definition: A general feature or nature that can belong to many separate things, such as being human.
The view that general natures are real outside our minds.
The view that general words do not need to match a shared thing existing outside the mind.
A feature that makes one thing this particular thing rather than another.
The study of how words, thoughts, and things are connected in meaning.

questions_to_think_about: When many things have something in common, does that shared feature exist outside our minds?
Can one word sensibly refer to many things without naming one shared object?
Can we know something perfectly without knowing every fact about it?

summaries.example: Consider the statement “Socrates is white.” Sharpe distinguishes the individual Socrates, the universal human nature, and the accidental form whiteness. A term such as “white” refers to a substance as a bearer of whiteness rather than directly naming the accidental form itself. This helps explain why Sharpe does not treat every apparently simple term as naming a simple entity.
summaries.summary: Johannes Sharpe was a philosopher and theologian associated with the Oxford Realists, a late-medieval movement influenced by John Wyclif. His central work, the Quaestio super universalia, presents arguments against and for universals, examines several historical positions, and then develops Sharpe’s own account. Sharpe is a realist: he holds that universal forms exist outside the mind in actual individuals. Yet he rejects the idea that language must mirror reality element by element. A term may be semantically universal because it signifies through one concept that refers to many things, even when no extra-mental common nature corresponds to it. This is especially important for terms such as “individual.” Sharpe’s metaphysics describes universals and individuals as really identical within one reality but formally distinct because their constitutive principles and properties differ. He revises Oxford realist accounts of predication, separating formal predication from predication by essence. He also develops views about individuation, the intellect, intelligible species, knowledge, and Aristotle’s natural philosophy. His work is therefore both a defense of realism and a substantial revision of realist methods in response to nominalist criticism.
key_ideas: Sharpe’s Quaestio super universalia surveys nominalist and realist positions before defending a revised form of Oxford realism.
He holds that real universals are really identical with individuals in a shared reality but formally distinct from them.
He makes semantic universality partly independent of the existence of an extra-mental common nature.
He distinguishes formal predication from predication by essence and links predication to identity and distinction.
He accepts intelligible species, maintains that each person has an individual intellect, and distinguishes perfect from complete knowledge.
In natural philosophy, he discusses matter, form, privation, the four causes, motion, place, time, continuity, divisibility, and heavenly motion.
summaries.why_it_matters: Sharpe’s philosophy illustrates a central problem in metaphysics and philosophy of language: how can general terms apply to many individuals, and what must the world contain for that to be possible? His answer refuses a simple choice between language as a mirror of reality and language as wholly detached from reality. By distinguishing real identity from formal distinction, he also offers a vocabulary for discussing entities that are inseparable in reality yet different in description, role, or constitutive principle.

important_terms.definition: A general nature or form that can be instantiated in multiple individuals; Sharpe holds that some universals exist extra-mentally in actual individuals.
A philosophical position affirming that common natures or essences have existence outside the mind.
A position denying that a common nature must exist outside the mind in order for a term to be general.
A mode of predication in which subject and predicate share some metaphysical components, without requiring the predicate-form to be directly present in the subject’s essence.
A relation in which entities share a reality but differ in their constitutive formal principles or properties.
The principle by which a common nature is instantiated in separate individuals; Sharpe connects it with matter affected by quantity and other accidents.
Sharpe’s account of how terms signify, including the role of a universal mode of signifying and the relation between concepts and things.
A representational principle required for intellection, according to Sharpe, allowing the intellect to understand universal essences.

questions_to_think_about: If a universal and an individual are really identical but formally distinct, what kind of difference remains between them?
Does Sharpe’s semantic account make it harder to justify his realism about universals?
Why might perfect knowledge of an object not require complete knowledge of all its properties?
Can a theory of language reasonably allow some general terms to lack a corresponding common nature in the world?
What does Sharpe gain by treating identity and distinction as matters that can have degrees?

summaries.example: Suppose a teacher says, “A student is waiting outside,” but does not say which student. The sentence gives a general description without identifying one particular person. Sharpe uses cases like this to think about words such as “individual.” He argues that such a term can be understood even when we do not know exactly which person it refers to, so it should not be treated as a name for one already-identified object.
summaries.summary: Johannes Sharpe was a philosopher and theologian of the late Middle Ages. He spent much of his academic life at Oxford and became one of the leading Oxford Realists, a group influenced by John Wyclif. The group debated nominalists about universals, which are general natures or features that may be shared by many individuals. Nominalists argued that generality belongs mainly to language or thought. Sharpe defended realism, saying that universal forms exist outside the mind in actual things. However, he accepted an important nominalist insight: language and thought do not have to copy the world in a perfectly direct way. For Sharpe, a term may be general because it signifies one concept that can refer to many things, even if no common nature exists outside the mind. He also argued that universals and individuals are really identical in a shared reality but formally distinct because they have different roles and constitutive principles. His work examines predication, identity, difference, individuation, the soul, knowledge, and Aristotle’s account of nature.
key_ideas: Sharpe belonged to the Oxford Realist tradition but revised it after considering nominalist criticisms.
He believed real universals exist in individual things and are also represented in thought and language.
He held that a word can be general because of how it signifies, not only because it names a shared nature.
He treated identity and distinction as related: things may share a reality while differing in formal features.
He argued that the mind can know individual material things and can know something perfectly without knowing it completely.
summaries.why_it_matters: Sharpe’s ideas show why questions about everyday language can become questions about reality. When we use one word for many things, we must ask whether those things share something real or whether the mind is organizing them. Sharpe’s position is especially interesting because it combines realism with a qualified acceptance of nominalist arguments. It demonstrates that philosophical disagreements can lead not only to choosing sides but also to developing a more complicated position.

important_terms.definition: A feature or nature that can be shared by several individual things.
The view that shared natures are real in the world, not merely ideas or words.
The view that general terms can work without matching a shared nature existing outside the mind.
A statement or relation in which one thing is said of another, as in “a human is an animal.”
A difference in the way two things are understood or structured, even when they are really the same in some important sense.
What makes one member of a kind a particular individual rather than another member of that kind.

questions_to_think_about: Are general words like “tree” connected to a real shared nature, or only to many similar objects?
Why might a philosopher think that language does not copy the world exactly?
How can two things be really identical in one respect but formally different in another?
What is the difference between recognizing something clearly and knowing every detail about it?
